content: Stilton is a type of cheese originating from England, available in two varieties: the well-known blue Stilton and the lesser-known white Stilton. Both varieties have been granted Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) status by the European Commission. This means that only cheese produced in the counties of Derbyshire, Leicestershire, and Nottinghamshire, and made according to strict guidelines, can legally be called Stilton. History The creation of blue Stilton is credited to Cooper Thornhill, the owner of the Bell Inn in the village of Stilton, located on the Great North Road. In 1730, Thornhill discovered a distinctive blue cheese during a visit to a small farm in rural Leicestershire. He was so impressed by the cheese that he arranged for exclusive marketing rights to sell it at the Bell Inn. Soon after, wagonloads of the cheese were delivered to the inn. Since Stilton village was located on the main stagecoach routes between London and northern England, Thornhill was able to promote the cheese effectively, and its reputation quickly spread. Manufacture and PDO Status Ironically, Stilton cheese cannot legally be made in the village of Stilton itself, despite the name. Historically, Stilton cheese was never produced in the village. Stilton is now part of Cambridgeshire, formerly in the county of Huntingdonshire. Currently, there are only six dairies licensed to produce Stilton cheese, all of which are regularly audited by an independent inspection agency accredited to European Standard EN 45011. Most of these dairies are located in the Vale of Belvoir, which straddles the Nottinghamshire-Leicestershire border. This area is considered the heartland of Stilton production, with dairies in villages such as Melton Mowbray, Colston Bassett, Cropwell Bishop, and Long Clawson. The only licensed dairy outside this area is in Hartington, Derbyshire, which owes its existence to a native of the Vale who purchased the dairy over a century ago. To qualify as blue Stilton, a cheese must meet the following criteria: It must be made only in the three designated counties using local milk that has been pasteurized. It must be produced in a traditional cylindrical shape. It must be allowed to form its own natural crust or coat. It must not be pressed. It must exhibit delicate blue veins radiating from the center. It must have a flavor profile characteristic of Stilton. Blue Stilton typically contains about 35% fat and 23% protein. Danish Blue cheese is made in a similar manner and also features the distinctive blue veining. Stilton Consumption Blue Stilton is often consumed with celery and is commonly used as a flavoring in vegetable soups, particularly cream of celery or broccoli soup. It is also eaten with crackers, biscuits, or bread. Traditionally, port wine is paired with blue Stilton. The cheese is especially popular during Christmas, which led to a 1990s advertising campaign featuring a person eating Stilton in March and declaring, It's traditional to eat Stilton at Christmas, followed by the phrase Merry Christmas. White Stilton, in contrast, does not have the Penicillium roqueforti mold introduced, which is responsible for the blue veining in blue Stilton. White Stilton is often blended with other ingredients, such as chocolate or dried fruit, or served with fruit cake. Huntsman cheese is a combination of blue Stilton and Double Gloucester cheese. Bizarre Dreams A 2005 study conducted by the British Cheese Board found that Stilton cheese could induce unusual dreams. Approximately 75% of men and 85% of women reported experiencing bizarre and vivid dreams after consuming a 20-gram piece of Stilton cheese 30 minutes before going to sleep. Stilton in Poetry The renowned British author G.K. Chesterton wrote essays on cheese, including one that lamented the absence of cheese in art. In one essay, he recounted a visit to the village of Stilton, which left a lasting impression on him. He expressed his experience through poetry in his Sonnet to a Stilton Cheese, which is partly a parody of Wordsworth's sonnet London, 1802.
